title: Attention operator scaling: Mistral / Qwen / Llama notes
body:
Purpose:
This is a scratchpad-style writeup of what we observed while profiling attention/GEMM/dispatch costs across three representative model families (Llama variants, Mistral-family checkpoints, and Qwen-ish encoder-decoder variants we have on the catalog). Goal: capture operator-level differences we saw on long-context workloads (2k–32k tokens) and MoE routing hotspots that affect latency SLOs on hosted and dedicated fleets.

Summary of headline findings (short):
- Attention operator is the dominant latency/memory knob at long context (>4k) for all models, but the failure modes differ by architecture.
- Mistral variants show higher sustained memory-bandwidth pressure in the attention forward/backward kernels; throughput falls earlier with sequence length than expected.
- Llama-style rotary models exhibit larger KV cache memory usage per token (dense kv layout), but attention computation scales more predictably with fused FlashAttention kernels we use.
- Qwen-ish models (our internal Qwen-adj test builds) show higher latency variance due to attention-layout + GELU/MLP pipelining differences; more sensitive to kernel launch overhead when sequence length is small but batch count is high.
- MoE routing cost (dispatch + combine) becomes the dominating CPU/GPU synchronization point when top-k routing is high or gating becomes imbalanced; naive dispatch produces tail latency spikes.

Experiment setup (notes):
- HW: A100 40GB, A100 80GB, and p4d (A100 nvlink) testbeds.
- Software: Runtime snapshot rc_2024_05_10 with FlashAttention-v2, cuBLAS 12.1, Triton kernels for fused MLP, and our in-house MoE dispatch CUDA kernels (branch: perf/moe-dispatch-optim).
- Models: Llama-13b and 70b (base Llama-style rotary), Mistral-8x (batch of model shims to approximate Mistral-like perf), Qwen-14B-ish test model. All quantized to 4/8-bit variants when noted.
- Workloads: seq_len = [512, 2048, 8192, 32768], batch sizes = [1, 4, 8], steady-state streaming scenario (prefix cached for repeated generation) and cold-start single-turn generation.
- Metrics captured: p50/p95/p99 latency (generation step), tokens/sec, GPU utilization, DRAM bandwidth (nvprof), kernel-level times (cuprof + tracer), and CPU-GPU memcpy time.

Detailed observations and traces:
1) Attention memory-bound vs compute-bound transition
- On 512–2048 tokens attention is typically compute-bound; our fused FlashAttention kernels show good utilization and scale with batch.
- Past ~4k tokens Mistral runs show a steep drop in tokens/sec: nvprof indicates memory bandwidth saturates (dram read BW near peak) on attention-Q/K/V gather/scatter passes. The symptom: kernels with lots of strided loads (rotary/rope differences?) have poor coalescing for Mistral's weight layout.
- Llama 70b maintained higher compute utilization with FlashAttention fused paths; the cache footprint is larger but the fused kernels reduce intermediate memcpy and temporary buffers, keeping bandwidth pressure lower relative to raw memory footprint.

2) KV cache layout differences and cost
- Llama-style: we allocate KV as contiguous HxSxD per layer which consumes more device memory at long context but allows contiguous GEMM-friendly ops when we slice per-head. The large contiguous allocation hurts when we need to duplicate caches for batching (cold starts) but allows faster pointer arithmetic for streaming.
- Mistral-style: observed more fragmented per-head storage in the vendor-provided checkpoints (after conversion), which increases kernel setup time and creates more small memcpy ops. This shows up in prof traces as many small kernels rather than a few big ones.
- Qwen: we saw a middle-ground layout; Qwen's positional encoding changes slightly altered the indexing math in the attention kernel which increased branch divergence on some kernels (raising p99).

3) Kernel launch overhead and small-batch behavior (Qwen sensitivity)
- When batch>1 and seq small (<1k), Qwen builds had relatively high kernel-count per step (attention split into more fine-grained kernels). Kernel launch latency (GPU side) and CPU orchestrator wakeups contributed to p95 latency growth.
- Mitigation in tests: combine smaller kernels with Triton-fused kernels and reduce CPU per-request work; reduced p95 by ~20% in our microbenchmarks.

4) MoE routing hotspots (observed on Mistral-MoE experimental builds and gated variants)
- Dispatch path: gather logits -> topk -> index-send (scatter) -> per-expert compute -> combine. Topk and scatter introduce both CPU and GPU synchronization. On imbalance, some experts are hot and cause queueing on GPU SMs.
- Profiling showed that topk selection (GPU->CPU roundtrip in naive implementation) cost up to 30% of generation step when routing topk>2 and batch>4.
- Our optimized path (all-GPU topk + preallocated expert buffers + async memcpy) reduced dispatch+combine cost by ~3-4x in steady state. However tail cases (rare tokens causing expert overload) still spike p99.

5) Quantization and attention numerics impact on kernel choices
- 4-bit quantization reduced memory pressure but increased compute overhead when dequantize-on-fly was used in the attention kernel. We saw a tradeoff: throughput gains at high seq for 4-bit in Llama due to lower cache pressure; Mistral's mem-bound attention sometimes did not benefit because extra dequantize ops increased memory access pattern complexity.

Open questions and TODOs (actionable experiments):
- Re-run the Mistral tests with converted layouts that coalesce per-head memory layout to see if bandwidth pressure reduces as hypothesized. (owner: Samir)
- Benchmark all-GPU topk vs host-side topk across p4d with nvlink disabled to simulate noisy neighbor scenarios (owner: Maya).
- Add a kerneled fused attention+kv-write that avoids intermediate buffers and measure reduction in DRAM write traffic on 8k+ contexts (owner: Jonas).
- Test MoE gating throttling: simulate synthetic expert skew to measure degradation curve and threshold where fallback to dense policy triggers. Need to capture p99 cost vs expert imbalance.

Quick checklist of mitigations that looked promising in microbenchmarks:
- Coalesce KV layout during conversion step for Mistral-like checkpoints. Reduced small memcpy count in trace.
- Switch Qwen small-batch attention to a larger Triton-fused kernel when seq<1k and batch>2. Reduces kernel launches.
- Implement all-GPU topk and use persistent per-expert buffers to avoid free/alloc churn.
- Introduce per-request dispatch budget and latency-aware routing to avoid sending large batches to a single hot expert (simple heuristic reduced p99 by ~18% in sim).
- Add a streaming-copy path for KV writes that uses cudaMemcpyAsync with pinned staging to reduce CPU blocking on cache writes.

Notes to self / heuristics learned:
- Watch for memory-bandwidth saturation first when profiling long-context drops in throughput. Compute utilization alone can be misleading.
- Kernel granularity matters: fewer, larger kernels reduce launch overhead and improve caching behavior on A100-like devices.
- MoE tail latency is often not visible in p50/p95 metrics; instrument p99/p999 and per-expert queue depth.
- Conversion scripts (hf->runtime) must include a layout canonicalization step for attention weights and KV allocation schema or we get many small memcpy kernels.

Short appendix: example flame trace summary (abstracted)
- Mistral-8x, seq=8192, batch=1: attention-forward kernels = 58% of step time, DRAM BW ~92% peak, many 1–3ms memcpy ops between kernels.
- Llama-70b, seq=8192, batch=1: attention-forward = 42% of step, fused kernels increased compute utilization, DRAM BW ~70%.
- Qwen-14b, seq=2048, batch=4: kernel-launch overhead + small GEMM fragments = p95 spike, attention-forward 35% but kernel-count ~150 per step.

End notes: this is a working doc. Will push a trimmed summary to confluence once we validate the conversion + all-GPU topk experiments. For now keep experiments and raw traces in perf bucket: gs://redwood-perf/attention/2024-05-attn-scan/
